Text: From January to August 2026, I took a career break to travel before returning to the job market, ready for a new challenge.

During my time at Enable, a startup fintech company, there was a constant issue of waiting for CI builds for the main, legacy solution. Build times could regularly take over 1 hour and 20 minutes. I led an initiative to investigate and attempt to decrease these build times, and through a number of small wins (e.g. removing unnecessary CI build steps that hadn't been looked at in a long time) and a few larger wins the build times were reduced by 50% to 40 minutes, with many hours of engineers being saved having to wait for these builds to finish.

The bigger wins included restructuring the complex testing to ensure integration tests were not being run when not necessary, as well as altering the build agents (virtual machines) which ran the CI pipeline - the bottleneck was not on the compute power of the build agents, but the number of agents, meaning more, lesser powered build agents was more efficient than fewer, higher powered build agents.

The CI platform was Azure DevOps.

In 2019/20, whilst at University, had the executive position of Tour Secretary in the University of Warwick Men’s Cricket Club. In this role I managed a combined £44,000 budget to organise a sports tour to South Africa. Unfortunately this trip was cancelled due to Covid-19, however I ensured that everyone on the trip got a full refund.

Whilst obtaining the refund was not particularly to do with me, this was a huge communication challenge, being the direct line of communication with the tour company and the touring group (22 university aged men). As well as this, I recognised challenges we faced, and what we could have done in the future to make our lives easier (such as obtaining group travel insurance, rather than lots of individual premiums, as well as using the university's credit card which would have given us greater financial protection).

Trainline ran the Pay As You Go (PAYG) trial for East Midlands Railway (EMR), which introduced a new problem: unlike Trainline's normal flow of billing before travel, PAYG users travelled first and were billed afterwards based on the journey they'd actually taken. This meant the systems that supplied UK fare data — traditionally built to answer "what does this journey cost right now" — needed to also answer "what did this journey cost N days ago," since we were the only team in the business that needed to look backwards rather than at current fares.

I took ownership of this fare retrieval problem: understanding how the industry fare data was structured and consumed across Trainline's legacy systems, and designing an approach to retain and serve a rolling window of historical fare data so the PAYG flow could always charge the correct fare for a journey after the fact. This meant extending systems that had never needed to preserve historical state in this way, while keeping current-fare lookups working exactly as before for the rest of the business. It was a cross-functional effort under a fixed deadline (the PAYG trial start date), delivered on time.

On top of this, due to the time constraints of the trial, a partial solution was implemented that would suffice for the initial months of the trial, due to the initial static nature of the fares. I also designed a longer-term solution designed to scale beyond the trial and oversaw a thorough handover of this project (in the form of detailed written documentation as well as in depth pairing sessions) to ensure understanding was not lost when I left Trainline.

Over several months, I worked closely with 3 junior engineers at Trainline, taking an active role in their onboarding and progression. This included regular 1:1 catchups and running workshops — for example, explaining how memory works at a basic level and practically what happens within C# in terms of memory allocation.

I enjoy playing guitar, cooking, staying active (playing cricket, rock climbing and running). I enjoy a challenge, as displayed with the Manchester marathon I ran in April 2025, for which I raised over £1,000 for Cancer Research UK. I was particularly proud of the marathon, as it was a culmination of many months of hard work, as well as overcoming a very early injury when I was trying to increase weekly mileage.

Alongside the technical work, I care about team culture and try to actively contribute to it. I introduced an optional Friday "casual hour" — an informal session to unwind and bond as a team before the week ended. I also organised in-person social activities such as curling.

As part of an experimentation team, I led an initiative to extend an existing trip-determination approach — originally built for the EMR PAYG trial — into new contexts it hadn't originally been designed for. This was highly iterative: several early assumptions about how well the original approach would generalise turned out to be wrong, which meant repeatedly revisiting the detection logic itself rather than just tuning existing parameters. To keep accuracy improving through these iterations, I introduced regression testing against real field data, so each change could be validated objectively rather than by intuition.
